cards.0.who: Every round, especially TA Linh (R1) and HM Khoa (R2). They score: clear, short, relevant to the role, and *tells a story* instead of reading out the CV.
cards.0.understand: This question isn't really about your background. The real question is *"Why should I keep listening to you?"*. You have 90 seconds to plant three things: (1) you design products of *trust*, (2) you have depth in both engineering and design, (3) you're heading toward exactly what Qualgo does. The most common mistake for someone with 14 years of experience: telling it in time order and running out of time at 2018.
cards.0.why: The opening line places you in 7 words (people remember a label, not a life story). The four stops show one thread running through everything instead of a list of jobs; one live number builds belief; the closing line answers "why us" before they ask. Where the question comes from: it shows up in 100% of interview rounds; Qualgo reviews confirm the TA opens with it.
cards.0.five: Under 100 seconds; the label "trust before use" in the first sentence; exactly one live number; end with Qualgo and Vietnam. The listener should be able to repeat your label after the session.
cards.0.evidence: ✅ 4 years as a developer + 10 years in product design. ✅ CYBERhythm 50% fewer errors. ✅ LSEG 190 countries (Eikon users, not "my product"). ✅ Fulfilment live, 24h → ~5 minutes. ✅ RegShield is an MVP. ✅ Stablecoin wallet, responsive web. ✅ Qualgo reached out 2 to 3 times.
cards.0.hook: "Trust before use" → 4 stops: Code · Cyber · Trader · Bank → Wallet → Home.
cards.0.image: On the reception desk sits a **small see-through safe**: you can see inside it (trust), it has a keypad (code), a radar screen (cyber), a candlestick chart (trader), a bank stamp (bank), and a tiny wallet sitting on top (wallet).
cards.0.locus: Room A, reception desk, object no. 1.
cards.0.must: (1) "products people have to trust"; (2) one live number (24h → ~5 minutes); (3) why Qualgo, why Vietnam.
cards.0.drill: Say 3 versions: 30 seconds, 90 seconds, 2 minutes. Record yourself. The 90-second version must not go over 100 seconds.
cards.0.traps: Starting from 2012. Saying "I'm passionate about…". Naming internal projects nobody knows (SLE, ExQual) in the first sentence. Calling the stablecoin wallet an "app". Going over 2 minutes.
cards.1.who: TA, HM, CEO. They score: did you do your research, do you understand the mission, or are you just running away from your current job.
cards.1.understand: Qualgo isn't famous. They know that. This question checks whether you have a *specific* reason or are just trying your luck. Because they reached out to you 2 to 3 times, you have a rare advantage: you can honestly say *you thought it through carefully* and didn't just jump in. Link it to the four principles (User first, Innovate with purpose, Act with transparency, G-local) without reciting them.
cards.1.why: The "three reasons in order of importance" structure shows you thought it through. The first reason is the user's problem (User first), the second is specific to Qualgo (it doesn't apply to other companies), the third is personal and honest (G-local). The detail "they reached out" turns you from an applicant into someone who was invited.
cards.1.five: The first reason is a problem for Vietnamese users (not yours), the second reason is only true for Qualgo, and the line "they reached out" is said as a fact, not to show off.
cards.1.evidence: ✅ scam figures (Tuổi Trẻ: about 18,900 billion dong in 2024; the 390,000 billion figure for 2023 is an estimate from a different organisation, be careful). ✅ Qualgo reached out 2 to 3 times. ✅ The G-local principle is from their careers page.
cards.1.hook: **P-S-H:** Problem · Shape · Home. "Phở, Sữa, Hẻm" (pho, milk, alley).
cards.1.image: On the desk is a **bowl of phở** (Problem: a hotpot full of scams), next to it a **milk carton with two compartments** (Shape: security + consumer), and a **Saigon alley sign** (Home).
cards.1.must: (1) scams "break the person, not the encryption"; (2) very few places do both security and consumer; (3) they reached out, and now the timing is right.
cards.1.drill: Say it without the word "passionate" and without the word "opportunity".
cards.1.traps: Reading out the mission word for word. Saying "great culture" when their Glassdoor rating is 3.1/5. Quoting scam figures you're not sure of. Giving salary or Saigon as the main reason.
cards.2.who: HM, HRBP, CEO. They score: are you running away, will you stay, do you speak badly about past employers.
cards.2.understand: The question behind it: *"If NAB is so good, why are you leaving? And will you leave us after 18 months?"* You've been at some places for 1 to 2 years (B12), so your answer has to show you're moving *toward* something, not running *away from* something. Your advantage: they reached out first.
cards.2.why: "Not wrong, finished" flips a negative question into a story about finishing. You name your awards (you're not running away), name what you want (you're moving toward it), and use the fact that they reached out first as proof you're not in a rush.
cards.2.five: Not one negative word about NAB; one piece of proof that you delivered (fulfilment live); the answer to the tenure doubt is ready before they ask.
cards.2.evidence: ✅ Q2 FY26 We Win Together, Q3 FY26 Individual Award. ✅ AI adoption lead since March 2026. ✅ Fulfilment live. 🟨 "hand over cleanly": only say it if it's true.
cards.2.image: On the desk is a **gift box tied with a bow** (finished), stamped *"Delivered"*, next to a **pair of honeycomb plastic sandals** (going home, consumer).
cards.2.must: (1) not running away; (2) delivered and done; (3) heading toward consumer, mobile, Vietnam.
cards.2.drill: Say the opening line 10 times until your voice is calm, not defensive.
cards.2.traps: Complaining about NAB, about managers, about restructuring. Saying "for growth" (empty). Saying "for money". Talking so much about RegShield that they think you're leaving it half done.
cards.3.who: HM, PM Mai, CEO. They score: how much research you did, how you reason when information is missing, honesty.
cards.3.understand: The product name isn't public. That's *a trap and a chance*. The trap: making things up. The chance: showing them how you reason from scattered signals, which is exactly the skill of someone building a new product. Structure: what I know for sure → what I infer → what I want to ask.
cards.3.why: The Know · Infer · Ask frame turns missing information into proof of product thinking. Reasoning from job listings is a trick few candidates use, and it makes a strong impression on the HM. The last line "correct me now" shows confidence that doesn't need to be right.
cards.3.five: At least one inference the interviewer hadn't thought of (from the job listings), and you invite them to correct you. If you already know the product name (Section 13.1 D1), say one specific thing you've tried in it.
cards.3.evidence: ✅ Description from the JD and the brand page. ✅ 17 open roles (agentic AI, iOS/Android lead, Go). ✅ The old Senior PD JD preferred chat experience. 🟦 Ask the recruiter for the product name *before* the HM round (see Section 13).
cards.3.hook: **Know · Infer · Ask** = "Biết, Đoán, Hỏi" (B-Đ-H, "Bánh Đúc Hành", rice cake with scallions).
cards.3.image: On the desk, three **glasses**: a clear glass (Know), a frosted glass (Infer), and a glass with a question mark carved into it (Ask).
cards.3.must: (1) three product groups; (2) inferences from their hiring (iOS/Android, agentic AI, chat); (3) three questions back.
cards.3.drill: Before the interview, update the "What I know" part with anything new (app store, LinkedIn, news).
cards.3.follow_ups.1.a: **"I'd want to know what it signals to a fifty-year-old in Cần Thơ before I'd have an opinion."**
cards.3.traps: Making up a product name. Saying "I couldn't find anything". Being too sure about your guesses. Bringing up Dubai without tact (save it for your questions back in Section 13).
cards.4.who: HM Khoa, Senior Designer Vy, CEO. This is the **deciding question** of the whole process. They score: are you self-aware, is your bridge convincing, do you have a plan to close the gap.
cards.4.understand: This is your no. 1 weak spot (2/5 on chat). There are three wrong answers: (1) denial ("enterprise and consumer are the same"), (2) apology ("you're right, I lack it"), (3) a list of generic skills. The right answer: **name the gap exactly + three strengths that carry over + proof you've started closing it + what you'll learn fast**. This is one of the four honest lines you must know by heart.
cards.4.why: Research on persuasion (inoculation, McGuire 1961; two-sided messages) shows that admitting a weakness first makes everything after it more believable. The three points go from the nature of the problem → evidence → action, and end with a team proposal instead of an apology.
cards.4.five: The honest line comes first, and your voice doesn't change when they push hard; your proof that you've started (P1, P2, P3) is ready to open; you end with a team proposal. The scorer writes: "gap acknowledged, mitigated".
cards.4.evidence: ✅ Honest line no. 1. ✅ CYBERhythm, stablecoin wallet, MICA capstone (mentorship platform), children's books. 🟦 Zalo/Telegram/Signal teardown and message request concept (Days 3 to 5 of the plan). **Only say the third point if you've done it.**
cards.4.hook: **"Haven't, but: Hard part · Not new · Started · Need"** = 4 fingers raised after a fist.
cards.4.image: On the desk, a **phone with a padlock** hanging over the screen (safe chat). You pick it up: the front shows chat bubbles (easy), the back shows security circuits (hard, and where you're strong).
cards.4.locus: Room A, object no. 5. This is the biggest object on the desk.
cards.4.must: (1) "I haven't shipped a consumer chat app"; (2) "the hard part isn't chat, it's trust"; (3) proof you've started learning.
cards.4.drill: Have a friend ask you this *in an aggressive voice* 5 times. You have to answer without speeding up.
cards.4.follow_ups.1.a: Open 4 screens. Talk about one decision, not everything.
cards.4.traps: Saying "UX is UX". Getting defensive. Talking too long (this is a question you could easily talk about for 4 minutes). Saying "I'm a fast learner" with no proof.
cards.5.who: TA Linh, HRBP Ngân. They score: consistency, gaps, directness.
cards.5.understand: The gap from June 2023 to Feb 2024 (B13) and the short stints will come up. A gap explained calmly is no problem. A gap you dodge is a red flag. 🟨 **You need to pick a true explanation** (finishing the MICA master's, the children's book, the 8-week UX programme, Toastmasters VP Education, a deliberate job search…).
cards.5.why: Telling it in chapters (not year by year) helps the listener remember; bringing up the gap yourself before they ask removes any sense that you're hiding something; "choosing, not taking the first offer" turns the gap into a deliberate decision.
cards.5.five: You bring up the gap before they ask, with an explanation you've checked, within 75 seconds.
cards.5.evidence: ✅ the dates. 🟨 **Explanation for the gap: confirm whether the 2022-23 milestones (children's book, UX programme 2023-24, VP Education 2023-24) really fall inside June 2023 to Feb 2024.** If not, give the real reason.
cards.5.hook: **Code · Security & Data · Pause on purpose · Bank.** "3 chapters + 1 comma".
cards.5.image: On the desk, a **book with three chapters**, and tucked between chapters 2 and 3 is a **bookmark shaped like a children's book**.
cards.5.must: (1) three chapters; (2) the gap, before they ask; (3) "choosing, not taking the first offer".
cards.5.follow_ups.0.a: **"Both were project-shaped roles. I moved when the scope I'd joined for was delivered. Looking back, I'd have stayed longer at one of them; I learn most in year two."** (includes one imperfect detail)
cards.5.traps: Not mentioning the gap and letting them find it. Saying "personal reasons" coldly (fine if it's true, but add one warm sentence). Describing every role in the same amount of detail.
cards.6.who: TA, HM, HRBP. They score: do you fit the role, is your ambition reasonable, will you stay.
cards.6.understand: They want to hear that you want exactly what they have, and that your future is *inside* their company. Don't say "Head of Design" too early if the Head of Product is interviewing you (it can feel like a threat). Talk about *impact* and *the team* instead of titles.
cards.6.why: The answer puts your future *inside* their product and talks about impact and people instead of titles, so it doesn't threaten the HM and still shows ambition.
cards.6.five: Your future sits inside their product; use honest line no. 4 when they ask about team size.
cards.6.evidence: ✅ Hearti Lab (team of 3), ADPList 250+ sessions, 50+ mentees, Tech Academy about 60 people.
cards.6.image: On the desk, a **bonsai tree** with two branches: the left branch holds a tiny phone (product), the right branch holds three tiny people (people). A brass name plate is stuck in the soil under the trunk, covered in dust (the title comes later).
cards.6.locus: Room A, object no. 7 (end of the desk).
cards.6.must: (1) consumer + trust; (2) building a team; (3) the title comes after the impact.
cards.6.follow_ups.0.a: **"Yes, when the product needs it. I've hired and led a team of three. I haven't run a team of ten yet, and I'd want to grow into that with the product, not ahead of it."** (honest line no. 4)
cards.6.traps: "Your job" (joking with the HM). "Start my own company". Answering only about titles.
cards.7.who: HM, Senior Designer Vy, PM Mai. They score: depth, your personal role, your thinking, results, and *why* you're proud.
cards.7.understand: Pick the project that shows the skill they need most, not the biggest project. For Qualgo: a project that is **live, has numbers, and has a hard decision about trust**. That's **Fulfilment at NAB CIB**. Your reason for pride should be a decision, not a number.
cards.7.why: It picks the live project with numbers over the biggest one; the reason for pride is a *decision* (where automation stops), which is what senior scorers rate highest; the last line links straight to Qualgo's anti-scam problem.
cards.7.five: The reason for pride is a decision (where automation stops), with "I" for the decision, "we" for the result, and a bridge to anti-scam.
cards.7.evidence: ✅ 24h → ~5 minutes, 80%+ validation, live. 🟨 "five teams": confirm the real number. 🟨 your "lead designer" role on this project.
cards.7.hook: **"The line"**: What not to automate. 24h → 5' · 80% · live.
cards.7.image: The **24** floor button in the lift is crossed out, with a **"5 minutes"** sticker stuck over it. A red painted line splits the lift floor in two: a robot on the left, a person on the right.
cards.7.must: (1) "what not to automate"; (2) 24h → ~5 minutes, live; (3) a link to anti-scam.
cards.7.drill: Tell a 60-second version and a 3-minute version.
cards.7.follow_ups.1.a: **"I'd have brought operations in a sprint earlier. We found two edge cases late that they'd have told us on day one."** (🟨 use the real detail)
cards.7.traps: Saying "we" all the way through with no "I". Taking credit for the automation. Using internal system names. Going over 3 minutes.
cards.8.who: HM, Vy, CEO. They score: UI craft, understanding of mobile, understanding of everyday users.
cards.8.understand: They're testing your biggest gap. Bring up the **stablecoin wallet** straight away, no apology, no going around in circles. Be clear about the stage (MVP, responsive web), but focus on *decisions* and *craft*.
cards.8.why: Opening straight with a consumer case, no detours, clears their biggest doubt. The insight "not use, dare" is the line people remember; the honest caveat at the end makes everything before it more believable.
cards.8.five: Open P1 or the wallet on a real phone, talk through one decision that had a fork in it, and give the honest caveat at the end. Never use the word "app" for the web version.
cards.8.evidence: ✅ 55 screens + admin, 2 DS, authentication research on about 18 apps (20 Jan 2026), Cursor. ✅ no native app yet. 🟨 whether you're allowed to mention "Humanity Centres". 🟨 whether you've declared it to NAB (T13).
cards.8.image: Button no. 2 shows an **open wallet**, and inside it are 18 app cards fanned out like a deck of playing cards. When you press the button, **a hand stops you right as you take money out**, not when you open the wallet.
cards.8.must: (1) "not use, dare"; (2) security at the moment of value; (3) the honest caveat.
cards.8.drill: Present it with 3 screens on a phone held in your hand, in 90 seconds.
cards.8.follow_ups.0.a: **"It's freelance work, outside my NAB hours."** 🟨 (add *"and declared"* only if it's true). **"If I join, I'd wrap it up before I start."**
cards.8.traps: "My app". "Users love it". Naming the client. Wandering off into stablecoins and blockchain (they do security, not crypto).
cards.9.who: Senior Designer Vy (very thorough), HM. They score: pure UI craft, taste, typography, detail.
cards.9.understand: Weak spot no. 3 (visual craft 3/5). Vy will zoom into the screen and check the spacing. Don't talk strategy here. Talk **pixels**: why this font, why this spacing, why this colour.
cards.9.why: Vy scores craft at pixel level: one system + one screen, a reason for each choice, plus the detail about Vietnamese with diacritics, shows you look at the right zoom level. The children's books are a rare detail that's easy to remember.
cards.9.five: Vy zooms into the Figma file and can't find a spacing mistake; you point out one thing you'd fix before she asks.
cards.9.evidence: ✅ 52 colours, 4.6/5, 100% task completion. ✅ children's books. 🟦 Have a Figma file ready that can be zoomed into, not just PNGs.
cards.9.image: Button no. 3 is a **round colour palette with 52 swatches**, and in the middle is a phone showing a huge money amount. At its base lies an **open picture book**.
cards.9.must: (1) one system + one screen; (2) a reason for each choice; (3) Vietnamese with diacritics.
cards.9.drill: Ask a designer friend to zoom into one of your screens and point out 3 mistakes. Fix them before the interview.
cards.9.follow_ups.0.a: always have one line ready: **"The secondary button competes too much. I'd drop it to a text link."**
cards.9.follow_ups.1.a: 🟨 Pick 2 real names/products you follow (for example Linear, Stripe, Revolut) and say *why* in specific terms.
cards.9.traps: Switching to talk about process. Showing a crowded dashboard. Saying "I'm more of a strategic designer" (Vy will write down "no craft").
cards.10.who: PM Mai, HM, Eng Hải. They score: accuracy, thinking about measurement, honesty about who caused what.
cards.10.understand: Every number on your CV will get dug into like this. This is honest line no. 2: *"That's measured, here's how…"* or *"That's an estimate, here's why I believe it."* Never leave a number without a definition. **🟨 You must fill in the real definition before the interview (T2).**
cards.10.answer_label: Sample answer (EN, frame; replace the parts in square brackets with the facts).
cards.10.why: This is honest line no. 2. The Define · Measure · Attribute · Label frame is how quantitative researchers answer; labelling a different number as an "estimate" yourself (60% AI) is the strongest honesty signal you can send.
cards.10.five: Define the number in one sentence, keep what's measured clearly apart from what's estimated, and say yourself which part didn't come from design.
cards.10.evidence: 🟨 **Definition of the 67% (you must fill this in).** ✅ ExQual 4.57 Platinum. ✅ RegShield 60% is an estimate.
cards.10.hook: **"Define · Measure · Attribute · Label."** (D-M-A-L, "Đi Mua Áo Lạnh", go buy a warm coat)
cards.10.image: Button no. 4 is a **tape measure** wrapped around the number 67. The end of the tape has a green **"measured"** label and a yellow **"estimate"** label.
cards.10.must: (1) the definition; (2) how it was measured; (3) design's part versus the team's part; (4) a label: measured or estimated.
cards.10.drill: Write a one-sentence definition for **each** number in the table of 12 numbers (Section 7.5).
cards.10.follow_ups.0.a: say the real number. If it's small: **"Small, about [N]. It's directional, not statistical."**
cards.10.follow_ups.1.a: **"The top tier of NAB's experience-quality scale."** 🟨 (confirm)
cards.10.traps: Being overconfident. Dodging. Bringing up a new number before you've answered about the old one. Saying "it was measured by the team" without knowing how.
cards.11.who: HM, Eng. They score: keeping "I" and "we" apart, not taking others' credit, not selling yourself short.
cards.11.understand: Senior people often say "we" (to be modest). The interviewer needs "I" to score you. Rule: **"We" for results, "I" for decisions.**
cards.11.why: "We" for results, "I" for decisions: the interviewer has something to score, and you still give the team credit. The closing line "the shape is mine" is short and confident.
cards.11.five: Three layers, Owned / Shaped / Others, with concrete examples, and one what-if line ("if I hadn't been there…").
cards.11.evidence: 🟨 check that every "owned/shaped" line is true for the project you pick.
cards.11.image: Button no. 5 has **three circles, one inside the other**: a dark core (owned), the middle ring (shaped), the outer ring (others).
cards.11.must: (1) three layers; (2) credit to engineering; (3) the closing line.
cards.11.drill: Apply the frame to all 3 portfolio cases.
cards.11.traps: "It was all team effort" (nothing to score). "I did everything" (nobody believes it).
cards.12.who: HM, HRBP, CEO. They score: self-awareness, ownership, learning, not blaming others.
cards.12.understand: It has to be a **real failure, caused by you, with consequences**, and you changed how you work after it. Don't pick a "fake failure" ("I worked too hard"). 🟨 **Pick a real story from your story bank (S1 to S20 in the Tech Academy Guidebook)**. The frame below uses a typical example; replace it with the facts.
cards.12.why: Interviewers judge a failure story on three things: it's real, you caused it, and you changed how you behave. The question "who opens this on a bad day?" is a concrete habit you carry with you, which proves the lesson is real.
cards.12.five: A real story with real consequences, a new habit you still use today, and a link to a later success.
cards.12.evidence: 🟨 **This is an example frame. Replace it with your real story.** Criteria: you caused it, it had consequences, it led to change, it links to a later result.
cards.12.image: Button no. 6 is **cracked**. A **little sprout** (the lesson) is growing out of the crack.
cards.12.must: (1) "I", not "we"; (2) a concrete consequence; (3) a new habit you still keep.
cards.12.drill: Prepare 2 different failure stories (one about product, one about people).
cards.12.follow_ups.1.a: the second story (🟨, for example feedback you gave a team member too late).
cards.12.traps: Blaming the client or the PM. Picking a failure that's too small. Picking a failure that's too big with no lesson.
cards.13.who: Security/AI Hằng, HM. They score: real understanding of security, not just buzzwords.
cards.13.understand: This is your strongest bridge to the core of Qualgo. Give three lessons, and make each one usable for consumer users.
cards.13.why: Three lessons boiled down into principles and then *moved straight over to consumer users*, which is exactly what Hằng wants to hear: you understand security from the human side, not from buzzwords.
cards.13.five: Each lesson is carried over to everyday users in the same sentence; Hằng doesn't hear a single buzzword you can't explain.
cards.13.evidence: ✅ CYBERhythm, 50% fewer errors, 10% faster, a data-viz library for 2 products. 🟨 the baseline and how it was tested (T9).
cards.13.hook: **Attention · Consistency · Scary state.** (A-C-S, "Ăn Cơm Sườn", eat rice with pork chop)
cards.13.image: Button no. 7 (the top one) is a **radar screen** with three bright dots: one red dot blinking (attention), three identical red dots (consistency), and one big dot in a panic (scary state).
cards.13.must: (1) three lessons; (2) 50% fewer errors; (3) each lesson applied to consumers.
cards.13.drill: Say the 3 lessons in 45 seconds with no examples; then in 2 minutes with examples.
cards.13.follow_ups.0.a: 🟨 name 2 real alert types (for example wrongly set access permissions, unusual logins).
cards.13.traps: Using security buzzwords you can't explain. Getting too technical. Not linking it to consumers.
cards.14.who: HM, Vy, PM (whiteboard round or 3-hour test). They score: process, asking questions, balancing safety with growth, craft, talking while you draw.
cards.14.understand: This is almost certainly the brief (or a version of it). They don't score pretty screens. They score **how you think out loud**. Use the **C-U-P-S-F** frame (Clarify, Users & risks, Principles, Sketch, Follow-up metrics), explained in detail in Section 12. This is the 2-minute spoken version to open with.
cards.14.why: Asking before you draw and naming the growth/safety tension are two senior signals that get their own score in the whiteboard rubric. The "waiting room" metaphor helps the whole room remember your idea in the debrief.
cards.14.five: Ask before drawing; give your ideas names ("Waiting room", "Call the saved number"); have a guardrail; never stay silent for more than 20 seconds.
cards.14.evidence: 🟦 Draw this brief 3 times, on Days 5, 9 and 12 (Section 14). Link: the Fulfilment case (where automation stops).
cards.14.hook: **"Waiting room, not living room."** 4 things: Inbox · Context card · Proportional risk · 3 actions.
cards.14.image: Whiteboard frame no. 1 shows a **house with a waiting room at the gate**, where a stranger sits on a red plastic stool holding a **card that says "how I know you"**. The light above the gate has 3 colours.
cards.14.must: (1) ask before drawing; (2) the growth/safety tension; (3) warnings that match the level of risk; (4) metrics + a guardrail.
cards.14.drill: Draw on paper, set a 30-minute timer, record your voice. Listen back: did you go silent for more than 20 seconds?
cards.14.traps: Drawing straight away. Designing only for safety (forgetting growth). Red everywhere. Forgetting the guardrail.
cards.15.who: PM Mai, HM. They score: understanding of cold start, network effects, privacy.
cards.15.understand: Chat onboarding means **"find my people safely"**, not a "feature tour". The hard part: growth needs contacts, but a brand that puts trust first can't vacuum up people's contacts the way Zalo does.
cards.15.why: Redefining chat onboarding as "find my people safely" shows you understand cold start and network effects; turning a legal requirement (Decree 147) into a trust moment is G-local thinking.
cards.15.five: Redefine onboarding as "find my people safely", make Skip a real choice, and bring a real observation from installing Zalo yourself.
cards.15.evidence: ✅ Authentication research on about 18 apps (stablecoin wallet). ✅ Decree 147. 🟦 Do the Zalo onboarding teardown (Day 3).
cards.15.hook: **Verify · Find · First chat · Defaults.** "V-F-F-D: Về Phố Phải Dè" (back in town, take care).
cards.15.image: Frame 2: a **door with a fingerprint lock** (verify) → a **contact list with a very big Skip button** → the first two chat bubbles → a **green switch** (defaults).
cards.15.must: (1) "find my people safely"; (2) Skip is a real choice; (3) the phone number isn't shown to strangers; (4) time to first message.
cards.15.drill: Install Zalo on a new phone (or a second account), screenshot every onboarding screen, and write down 3 things you learned and 3 things you'd do differently.
cards.15.traps: A 4-screen intro carousel. Forcing contact sync. Forgetting network effects.
cards.16.who: Mobile Eng Tuấn, Vy. They score: platform knowledge, design systems, engineering reality.
cards.16.why: "Consistent meaning, native behaviour" is the line mobile engineers want to hear; stressing that security flows must be identical on every device is a detail only someone who works in security would think of.
cards.16.five: You list five platform differences smoothly and point to P1 with the same flow on iOS and Android.
cards.16.evidence: ✅ 2 design systems on one structure. ✅ A small design system at Hearti Lab. 🟨 hands-on experience with platform-specific component variants.
cards.16.hook: **"Same meaning, native behaviour"** · 3 layers: Shared · Adapted · Unique.
cards.16.image: Frame 3: **three áo dài** with the same pattern (shared), but one is iOS blue, one is Android green, and one is as wide as a desktop screen.
cards.16.must: (1) same meaning, native behaviour; (2) security flows must be identical; (3) one spec with variants.
cards.16.drill: Learn 5 iOS/Android differences by heart (back, tab/nav bar, FAB, share, notifications).
cards.16.traps: "Pixel-perfect same on all platforms". Not knowing predictive back or Dynamic Type.
cards.17.who: PM, HM, Vy. They score: structured thinking, understanding of users' mental models.
cards.17.why: It starts from the user's question ("who will see this?") instead of the menu structure; showing the audience in the message box is a concrete design idea that's easy to remember and can be tested.
cards.17.five: The "who will see this?" question and the idea of showing the audience in the composer, with a sitemap in P1.
cards.17.evidence: ✅ MICA capstone (mentorship platform, community). ✅ Knowledge from Section 9.1. 🟦 Compare the IA of Telegram and WhatsApp Communities.
cards.17.image: Frame 4: a **megaphone** (channel), a **round dinner table** (group chat), an **apartment block** (community). Above the message box, the words **"3,240 people will see this"** glow red.
cards.17.must: (1) the "who will see this" question; (2) three types by size + direction; (3) the audience shown in the composer; (4) card sort/tree test.
cards.17.traps: Too many tabs. Forgetting phone number privacy in communities.
